prompt: Two ordinary threads run inside one process. Assume ordinary non-thread-local globals and no escaped references to local variable storage. Which resources belong to the shared process rather than being automatically duplicated per thread? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Any heap object reachable from both threads can be read and written by both; this is the source of both the speed and the bugs.
Correct. Globals live in the process's memory, not in any one thread.

options.text: Local variables of a function each thread is running
options.explanation: Each thread has its own stack, so each call has distinct local storage; a language may still permit sharing its address. (The objects they *point to* may still be shared.)
Each thread has its own stack; that is what lets them be at different points in different functions.
Correct. File descriptors belong to the process, so a socket opened by one thread can be used by another.

workedExample:
Sort each item by where it lives:

| Item | Lives in | Shared? |
|---|---|---|
| Heap object | Process heap | Yes |
| Global | Process data | Yes |
| Local variable | Thread's stack | No |
| Call stack | Per thread | No |
| Open socket | Process table | Yes |

A subtle case: distinct local storage need not enforce isolation if its address escapes; but if it holds a reference to a heap list, the *list* is shared if another thread has a reference too.
